posts.text:
The avatar engine with the most realistic demo is usually one you cannot put in a product. Most of the highest-fidelity work in this field is research code under a non-commercial license.

The Avatar Engines Atlas maps 24 engines and puts each license next to the technique. Turn on the commercial-use filter and 5 remain.

three.ws/avatar-engines

Each card states what the engine takes in, what it outputs, what it runs on, and what its license permits.

For several photorealistic engines the gate is compute, not the license. A training run per subject is not something you put behind a button.

2 of the 24 are live on the platform today: the MIT-licensed generator behind the free text and image to 3D lane, and the skeleton the animation pipeline canonicalizes against.

Filters are written into the URL, so a filtered view is a link you can share.

posts.text:
Herald decides whether a message is worth interrupting you for before a word of it is said. Each message carries an importance, the page sets a floor, and the engine returns a verdict.

We sent one at 80 against a floor of 50 and it was delivered: the 3D character in the corner of the page said it. We sent the next at 29. The character said nothing, and the verdict came back as a drop with its reason: below-importance-floor.

Every message that is not delivered comes back with a reason, so why you were not told has an answer.

three.ws/herald

A drop and a hold are different verdicts.

A held message is delivered once the thing blocking it clears: another message on screen, a tab in the background, a full rate limit, quiet hours. A dropped one is reported with its reason and will not be delivered.
A verdict of deliver is what makes the 3D character speak, with the gesture the sender chose. On a page with no GPU the same verdict arrives as a card, in a live region, dismissible with Escape.

posts.text:
A Gaussian splat rebuilds a person or a room as millions of tiny blobs instead of polygons. The splat viewer decodes one on your own device and draws it in a browser tab with WebGL, so the file stays with you.

Paste a link to a capture or drop the file in. It reads five formats and tells them apart by their bytes, not their filenames.

Both built-in samples are synthetic. They exist to exercise the renderer and are not real captures. A real one comes out of a capture engine trained on footage of a person, exported as a file, then opened here.

three.ws/splat

To share a capture, add ?src= and the address of the file to the address of the viewer. The scene loads as the page opens, so the link is the whole handoff.

The same scene that is a 1 GB PLY is roughly 100 MB as SPZ, which is the difference between a capture you can send as a link and one you cannot.

posts.text:
An avatar manifest that carries the SHA-256 of the mesh it was built from, so a model re-exported or swapped under the same filename fails your build instead of your page.

three-ws-avatar reads the GLB once and writes its digest and size into the manifest, then validates the whole document against the published schema. Four commands, one runtime dependency, no network calls, so it runs offline inside a release script.

preview prints the two lines of HTML that embed the avatar. The page pastes them in unmodified, and the viewer on it is that markup rendering.

validate exits non-zero on an invalid manifest and prints each error at the path where it happened, so a bad file fails the build step instead of logging a warning. hash prints the digest alone on stdout, which makes the drift check a one-line comparison.

Install line, the four commands, and the manifest fields: three.ws/avatar-cli
The owner is a chain-scoped account, so ownership is unambiguous off-platform. A Solana address is accepted as is.

posts.text:
A checksum tells you two GLB files differ. It cannot tell a lossless re-export from a rig that quietly lost joints, and only one of those takes your avatar off the screen.

Model Diff reads both files and reports the change set: geometry, materials, textures, skeletons and animation clips, with renames and moves detected the way git detects them. Both files are parsed and compared in your browser. Nothing is uploaded.

In the reel, two different characters: the verdict is breaking, with 2 joints lost, 5 animations removed and 4 objects renamed rather than rewritten. three.ws/diff

Severity is one of none, cosmetic, minor, major, breaking, so a build can gate on it. Breaking means something a consumer references by name is gone: a clip, a joint, a mesh. That is the failure that renders fine and never moves.

Vertex data is compared at a quantum of 1e-4 units, so the float drift of a re-export does not register while a genuine edit does.

The same engine runs this page, the CLI and the free API, so a verdict in CI cannot disagree with what you see here. The package is three-ws/glb-diff on npm: hand the CLI two files and a --fail-on level, and the build fails on the severity you choose.

posts.text:
A nine-cylinder radial engine and a steam locomotive, with no model file behind either one. It is a Labs experiment in building 3D geometry from code instead of files.

Both machines are built when the page loads: dimensions become profiles, profiles get revolved or extruded, and the results are merged into the parts you can see. Move a slider and the geometry is rebuilt. Nine cylinders to five, and the displacement readout, the parts list and the source panel follow, because all of them are derived from the same numbers.

The motion is solved, not baked animation. Pistons come from the exact planar slider-crank, and the locomotive valve gear closes a four-bar chain by intersecting circles every frame, which is why a rod length that cannot physically reach refuses to move rather than stretching.

Each machine is a small JSON object of numbers. Copy the spec, hand it to an agent, get a different machine back, then export the result as GLB. three.ws/assembly

posts.text:
4,672 triangles, 19 joints, 1 animation, 0 validator errors and 1 warning. One GET request told us that about a 3D file, with no API key and no account.

The inspect endpoint is free. Hand it the address of a glTF or GLB and it answers in JSON: whether the file is valid, what is inside it, and a prioritized plan to make it smaller and faster.

It is built for AI agents that make or buy 3D mid-task and need to know what they got before they use it.

Send the address in a GET, or POST the file itself. The cap is 32 MB a file and 60 requests a minute.

It reports up to 10 validator findings, each with its code and where in the file it sits, beside the true totals.

The spec is OpenAPI 3.1, so an agent can read it and call this on its own: three.ws/3d

posts.text:
Pick a model, or drop your own .glb, and the inspector runs the exact quality gate our catalog applies to its own entries: same module, same thresholds, same decision. It runs in your browser, and the file never leaves your machine.

Every rule shows what it measured against its bound, and a failed rule comes with the fix. The mannequin in the reel is 2 checks short: no texture, and 22 meshes where a character may have at most 8, so it will not rig or animate as one body.

Switch the category to Prop and the assembled-character rule stops applying, because loose parts are legitimate on a prop. Michelle from the library is a clean pass. Fox passes, barely. Copy any verdict as JSON or as a shareable link. three.ws/inspect

posts.text:
Pick what you want to make, copy the prompt, paste it into Claude, and swap the words in angle brackets for your own.

That is the whole Prompt Library: 24 prompts, each written to produce something real, like a 3D model you can download or a live avatar on your page. 15 of them need nothing installed.

10 are for making 3D: a model from a sentence, a rigged avatar from a description, a rig for a GLB you already have.

Each prompt names the tools to call and what to check before it answers. The rigged avatar one has Claude look at the rendered frames and fix the proportions before it says it is done.

The library is also published as plain text and as JSON, so an agent can read it too.
